client: I've been really stressed out lately because I missed the deadline for my final project at university, and I can't stop thinking about how badly it's going to affect my grade. Every time I sit down to try to work on it or even just think about what to do next, I just freeze up and my mind goes blank. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to fix anything, because the damage is kind of already done, you know?
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy mix of dread and helplessness right now — that sense of being stuck even when you want to move forward is really exhausting. You're right that we can't undo the missed deadline, but I'm curious whether the story you're telling yourself about *how bad* the damage is might be adding an extra layer of weight on top of the actual situation. What's the worst outcome you're imagining, and how certain do you feel that it's definitely going to happen?

client: The worst outcome I keep picturing is failing the whole course, which could delay my graduation and just completely derail everything I've been working toward. I'd say I feel pretty certain it's going to happen, like maybe 80 or 90 percent sure, even though I know I'm probably catastrophizing. But even if it's not that extreme, a really bad grade still feels like proof that I'm not cut out for this, and that thought is hard to shake.
therapist: That thought — "this proves I'm not cut out for this" — is really worth gently examining, because it's doing a lot of heavy lifting in how you're feeling right now. One missed deadline becoming evidence of your entire worth and capability is a thinking pattern we call overgeneralization, and it tends to feel absolutely convincing even when the evidence doesn't fully support it. What would you say to a close friend who missed a deadline and was telling themselves the same thing?

client: I'd probably tell a friend that one mistake doesn't define them and that they should just talk to their professor and figure out next steps. But it feels different when it's me, like I know logically that's the right thing to say but I can't actually make myself believe it when I'm the one in the situation. It's almost like there's a double standard I'm holding myself to and I can see it but I still can't get out from under it.
therapist: It's actually a really meaningful moment of self-awareness that you can see the double standard clearly — that gap between what you'd offer a friend and what you allow yourself to believe is something a lot of people never even notice. The fact that you *can* articulate the kinder perspective means it's in there somewhere, even if it doesn't feel emotionally true yet, and that's something we can work with. What do you think makes you feel like you deserve less compassion or understanding than you'd give someone else in the exact same situation?

client: I think part of it is that I feel like I should know better, like I've been in university long enough that missing a deadline isn't something that should happen to me. There's this voice in my head that says other people have just as much going on and they manage to get things done, so my struggling with it means there's something specifically wrong with me. I'm not sure where that comes from but it's been there for a long time, way before this deadline thing happened.
therapist: That voice sounds like it's been a quiet but persistent companion for a long time, and it's worth noticing that it's built on a comparison to an imagined version of "other people" who are somehow handling everything perfectly — which is rarely the full picture of anyone's reality. The belief that struggling means something is *specifically wrong with you* is one worth really questioning, because it sounds less like a fact and more like an old story you picked up somewhere along the way. Do you have any sense of where that story might have started — was there a time earlier in your life when you first learned that needing help or falling short meant something was fundamentally wrong with you?

client: Honestly, yeah, I think it probably goes back to when I was younger and school was the main thing I felt like I was good at, so any time I didn't do well it felt like a really big deal. My parents weren't harsh about it or anything, but I could tell they were proud of my grades and I think I just internalized that my value was tied to performing well. I'm not sure how useful it is to dig into all of that right now though, because it doesn't really change the fact that I still have this project hanging over me and I don't know what to do about it.
therapist: You've just made a really important connection — that sense of "my worth equals my performance" didn't come from nowhere, it was something you quietly learned as a way to feel secure, and it's been running in the background ever since. And you're absolutely right that the project still needs to be dealt with, so let's honor both things — the deeper pattern *and* the practical next step. Given that you already know what you'd tell a friend in this situation, what feels like the smallest possible first move you could make today, even something as simple as drafting an email to your professor?

client: Drafting an email to my professor sounds simple enough but every time I think about actually doing it I get this wave of anxiety, like I don't even know how to explain myself without sounding like I'm making excuses. I'm also kind of scared of what the response might be, because if they're unsympathetic or the answer is just no, I think that would make me feel even worse than I do now. So I guess I'm worried that taking that step could actually backfire and make things harder to cope with.
therapist: That anxiety makes a lot of sense — you're essentially weighing the discomfort of uncertainty now against the risk of a painful answer later, and your mind is trying to protect you by avoiding the step altogether. But it's worth noticing that right now you're already living with a difficult feeling, and the "what if they say no" scenario is actually no worse a situation than the one you're already in — you'd just have more information to work with. What do you think would actually happen inside you if you sent the email and the response wasn't what you hoped — do you think you'd be able to cope with that, even if it was hard?

client: I think I probably could cope with it, but in the moment it would feel really devastating and I'd likely spiral into that whole "this proves I'm not good enough" place again. I guess what scares me is not just the practical outcome but how I'd feel about myself afterward, like a rejection from my professor would become more than just a no about an extension, it would feel personal. I can see that's probably not a rational way to look at it, but knowing that doesn't make the fear feel any smaller.
therapist: You're showing real insight by recognizing that a professor's response would get filtered through that old story about your worth — that's exactly the pattern we'd want to gently interrupt if the difficult moment came. And you're right that knowing something isn't rational doesn't automatically dissolve the fear, but what it *does* give you is a small moment of choice — a chance to notice the spiral starting and ask whether a professor's email is really a verdict on who you are. If that hard moment did come and you noticed yourself sliding into "this proves I'm not good enough," what's one thing — even tiny — that might help you challenge that story in that moment rather than getting swept away by it?

client: Maybe I could try reminding myself of that friend thing, like asking what I'd say to someone else in the same situation, because at least earlier when I thought about it I could access a kinder perspective even if it didn't fully stick. But I'm a bit skeptical that in the middle of a spiral I'd actually have the presence of mind to do that, because when I'm really anxious my thoughts just move so fast and it's hard to slow down enough to catch them. I guess it's worth trying, but I don't want to set myself up to feel like a failure again if I try the technique and it doesn't work in the moment.
therapist: It's really encouraging that you've already identified something that could help, and the fact that you're thinking ahead about its limitations actually shows a lot of self-awareness rather than defeat. It might help to reframe the goal slightly — instead of "successfully stopping the spiral," the aim could simply be to *notice* it a little sooner each time, even if you still get swept up, because that tiny pause is genuinely a skill that builds gradually rather than something that works perfectly right away. And importantly, if you try it and it doesn't fully work in the moment, that wouldn't be another failure — it would just be useful information about what you need, so how does it feel to think about measuring success by the attempt rather than the outcome?

client: That framing actually does feel a little less pressure-filled, like it takes away the pass-or-fail quality that I tend to attach to everything. But I notice I'm a bit suspicious of it too, because it almost sounds too forgiving, like a way of lowering the bar so I never really have to push myself. I think part of me worries that if I'm too easy on myself about the process, I'll just use it as an excuse to avoid actually dealing with the hard stuff.
therapist: That tension you're naming is really common and actually quite healthy — it shows that you care about growth and don't want self-compassion to become a hiding place. But there's an important distinction between lowering the bar and simply removing the punishment, because what we're really doing is making it *safer* to attempt hard things rather than letting you off the hook for doing them. What if self-compassion and pushing yourself aren't actually opposites — can you think of a time when feeling less afraid of failure actually helped you take a harder step rather than avoid it?

client: Actually, yeah, there was a time in my first year when I was really struggling with a subject and I finally just admitted to a study group that I didn't understand the material, and because I wasn't terrified of looking stupid in front of them I actually ended up getting through it okay. So I guess there is something to what you're saying, because that felt like a situation where not punishing myself for not knowing things made it easier to actually ask for help. I hadn't connected that to this situation before, but I can see how it might be relevant to sending that email.
therapist: That's a really powerful connection you just made entirely on your own — you already have lived evidence that self-compassion opened a door rather than closed one, and that's not a small thing. It sounds like something has shifted a little in this conversation, like you've moved from feeling completely stuck to being able to see a possible path forward, even if it still feels uncertain. Given everything you've reflected on today, how are you feeling about the idea of drafting that email to your professor — does it feel any different now than it did when we first mentioned it?
